entries.topic: 'Israel' and 'Palestine' in the ancient record: the stelae, Herodotus, Rome and the caliphate

claims.text: The earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible is on a victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah, dated c. 1207 BCE, found by Flinders Petrie in 1896 in the first courtyard of Merneptah's mortuary temple at Thebes; it is now in the Cairo Museum.
The stele's line on Israel uses a stock phrase for a conquered place, rendered 'Israel is wasted, its grain (or seed) is not'.
The scribe marked 'Israel' with a determinative (an unpronounced sign) for a people or ethnic group, while names such as Ashkelon and Gezer carry the sign for a place.

The Tel Dan stele, an Old Aramaic inscription of c. 840 BCE (mid-ninth century by its script), was found in 1993 at Tel Dan in northern Israel during excavations under Avraham Biran; two smaller fragments followed the next year. It is held at the Skirball Museum, Jerusalem.

An Aramaean king, most likely Hazael of Damascus, boasts on the Tel Dan stele of victories over the king of Israel and the 'House of David'; line 9 is the earliest known mention of David's dynasty outside the Bible.

The Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), c. 840 BCE, written in Moabite, was seen in 1868 by the missionary F. A. Klein near Dibon in Transjordan; it states that 'Omri was the king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab for many days'. It is now in the Louvre.
The earliest surviving text to use the name Palestine is Herodotus's Histories (second half of the fifth century BCE), which speaks of 'Syria Palaistine' for the coast between Phoenicia and Egypt.

Herodotus (Histories 2.104.3) also mentions 'Syrians who are in Palestine' who practise circumcision; Philo of Alexandria (d. c. 50 CE) and Josephus (c. 93–94 CE) both used 'Palestine' in writing about Jews.

The Greek name is generally linked to the Philistines (Hebrew peleshet), an Aegean people who settled the southern coastal plain in the twelfth century BCE; Bowersock calls the older variant forms (Peleset, Phlishtu) etymologically obscure.

Roman inscriptions show that around the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–136 CE) Judaea was merged with Galilee into a province called Syria Palaestina; no ancient source states when or why the change was made.
Under Byzantium the region was divided into First, Second and Third Palestine; after the Muslim conquest First Palestine became Filastin and Second Palestine became al-Urdunn.
Under the Umayyad caliph 'Abd al-Malik (late seventh century) Palestine existed as a province of the caliphate, Jund Filastin.

In Ottoman times 'Palestine' was an informal term, not the name of a province; the word 'Palestinian' for Arabic speakers is attested from 1898 (Khalil Baydas), and Ruhi al-Khalidi wrote on 'the Palestinian race' in the newspaper Filastin in 1913, according to Zachary Foster as cited by the Jewish Virtual Library.

disputes.question: Did Hadrian rename Judaea 'Palaestina' to punish the Jews and erase their tie to the land?

positions.view: Yes, probably: Louis Feldman (1990) argued Hadrian was the likely author, given his decrees against Jewish national and religious life, while conceding that only circumstantial evidence links him to the change.

Not established: the name was already in Greek and Latin use for centuries, including by Jewish writers; Ronald Syme suggested the change may have come in 130 CE, before the revolt, and David Jacobson (1999) and others read it as administrative or Hellenizing rather than punitive.

disputes.question: Is there continuity of a 'Palestine' and a Palestinian people over four thousand years?

positions.view: Nur Masalha (Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History, 2018) argues that Palestinian place-names and identity persisted through Roman, Byzantine and Islamic rule.

G. W. Bowersock, reviewing Masalha, calls the four-thousand-year title indefensible: the documented name begins with Herodotus, and its location and meaning kept changing; he nonetheless praises the book's erudition.
The Jewish Virtual Library argues the name was Roman-imposed and that Palestinian nationalism dates from the 1910s–1920s as a reaction to Zionism.

entries.topic: Antisemitism as a hatred, before the word: the blood libel, badges and expulsions, Damascus 1840 and the Protocols

claims.text: The blood libel, the accusation that Jews kill Christians to use their blood, has its first medieval case at Norwich, England, in 1144, after the body of a boy named William was found in the woods; earlier references occur in the writings of Apion.

Further ritual-murder accusations followed at Gloucester (1168), Blois (1171), Saragossa (1182), Bristol (1183), Fulda (1235), Lincoln (1255) and Munich (1286); in the fourteenth century the charge was combined with accusations of well-poisoning during the Black Death.

At Trent in 1475, after a two-year-old named Simon disappeared, the town's Jews were tortured into confessing and burned; the Catholic Church removed Simon from the list of saints and repudiated the charge in 1965.

The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) decreed distinguishing dress for Jews and barred them from public office; England was the first country to require a Jewish badge (1218), and church leaders at Osney Abbey near Oxford adopted their own badge decree in 1222, when about 3,000 Jews are thought to have lived in England.

England's 1275 Statute of Jewry barred Jews from living among Christians; in 1290 Edward I expelled the Jews of England, the first such expulsion in Christendom. Jews were permitted to return in 1656, under Cromwell.

On 5 February 1840 the Capuchin friar Thomas and his servant disappeared in Damascus; the Capuchins accused the city's Jews of ritual murder, the French consul Ratti-Menton backed the investigation, two of the accused died under torture and 63 Jewish children were seized to pressure their mothers.

Muhammad Ali ordered the torture stopped on 25 April 1840; after a mission by Moses Montefiore and Adolphe Crémieux, the surviving prisoners were freed on 28 August 1840 without a declaration of innocence, and the Ottoman Sultan issued a firman repudiating the ritual-murder charge.

The Kishinev pogrom began on Easter Sunday, 19 April 1903, after articles in an antisemitic newspaper; almost 50 Jews were killed over three days. In 1911–13 Menachem Mendel Beilis was tried in Kiev on a ritual-murder charge and acquitted.

The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated plan for Jewish world domination, was first serialized in the St Petersburg newspaper Znamya in autumn 1903 and appended by Sergei Nilus to a book in 1905.

In 1920 Henry Ford's Dearborn Independent ran a 91-part series based on the Protocols; in August 1921 The Times of London showed the text was largely copied from Maurice Joly's 1864 satire and called it a forgery; Ford apologized in 1927.
Hitler cited the Protocols in Mein Kampf (1925), the year the first Arabic translation appeared in Damascus; a Swiss court in Bern ruled against its publishers in 1935.

The Protocols kept circulating after the war: an Iranian English edition (1985), Article 32 of the 1988 Hamas charter, a 41-part Egyptian television series (2002), a Hezbollah Al-Manar series (2003); a Russian court ruled it a forgery in 1993.
In 1943 Hajj Amin al-Husseini, the former Mufti of Jerusalem, echoed the Protocols' themes in Arabic broadcasts from Berlin.

entries.topic: The departure of the Jews of the Arab world, country by country: Libya, Egypt, Syria, Aden, Bahrain, Algeria

claims.text: Libya had about 21,000 Jews in 1911 (about 4% of 550,000 people) and 30,387 on the eve of the Second World War; Italy's 1938 racial laws were enforced there from 1940, and by June 1942 some 2,584 Jews had been deported to the Giado camp, where 562 died.

A three-day attack on the Jews of Tripoli in November 1945, under British military administration, killed 120 Jews and destroyed at least five synagogues; riots in 1948 killed 12 more and destroyed 280 homes.

According to Yad Vashem, 30,972 Libyan Jews emigrated to Israel in the wake of the violence around 1948; a 1961 law denied nearly all Jews proof of citizenship, about 6,000 were airlifted to Rome after the 1967 riots, and by 2004 no Jews remained in Libya.

Egypt's Jewish community numbered an estimated 75,000–80,000 at its height in 1948 (Israeli Foreign Ministry estimate); bombs in Cairo's Jewish quarter between June and November 1948 killed more than 70 Jews.

During the Suez war, from 29 October 1956, the Egyptian government treated Jews as enemies of the state: about 1,000 were arrested in Cairo, 450 Jewish-owned businesses were confiscated, and from 15 November departing Jews had to sign forms renouncing property and Egyptian citizenship (per Joel Beinin and an AJC factsheet of March 1957).
About 25,000 Jews left Egypt in 1956, leaving roughly 15,000 in 1957, according to figures cited by the University of Washington's Stroum Center.

After the UN partition vote of 29 November 1947, rioters in Aleppo on 30 November damaged the Great Synagogue and the tenth-century Aleppo Codex and destroyed some 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues, according to the Center for Israel Education.

In British-ruled Aden, rioting from 2 December 1947 killed 82 Jews and wounded 76; in Manama, Bahrain, on 5 December the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman killed, according to the Center for Israel Education.

Algeria's Jews received French citizenship by the Crémieux Decree of 24 October 1870; Vichy withdrew it on 7 October 1940 and it was restored on 20 October 1943. Rioting in Constantine in 1934 killed 25 Jews.

Of about 140,000 Algerian Jews in the mid-1950s, almost 130,000 moved to France at independence in 1962; 25,681 Algerian Jews immigrated to Israel from 1948 on, according to the Jewish Virtual Library.
Totals are given differently by different advocates: Avi Beker (Jewish Political Studies Review) gives about 900,000 Jews 'forced out' of Arab countries, of whom about 650,000 went to Israel.

disputes.question: Were the Jews who left the Arab world 'refugees' comparable to the Palestinian refugees of 1948?

positions.view: Yes: Avi Beker and the 'dual refugee problem' position (H. Con. Res. 311, October 2003) hold that about 900,000 Jews were forced out of Arab countries and that their case has been forgotten through international indifference and Israeli reluctance to call it expulsion.

No: the Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav (Haaretz, 2006) argued that Palestinians did not leave of their own volition, while Arab Jews moved to Israel under state and Jewish-organization initiatives, some willingly and some not; the Palestinian writer Khalid Amayreh (Ahram Online, 2012) called the equation propaganda meant to offset the Nakba.

Between them: the Stroum Center essay treats the 1956 Egyptian departures as expulsion, while warning, with the historian Eyal Bizawe, against using Mizrahi history to cast Arab societies as permanent enemies; it asks that coexistence be taught alongside the expulsions.

entries.topic: The land's other communities: Druze, Bedouin, Circassians and Samaritans

claims.text: The Druze faith took shape in the Middle Ages and has accepted no converts since the eleventh century; about 150,000 Druze live in Israel proper in eighteen villages, and about 24,000–25,000 in the Golan Heights, according to Minority Rights Group.

Israel's Druze population grew from 14,500 in 1949 to about 152,000, according to Central Bureau of Statistics figures reported in April 2024; the largest Druze localities at the end of 2022 were Daliyat al-Karmel and Yarka, each with over 17,000 people.

Druze in Galilee and on Mount Carmel fought alongside the Jewish forces in 1948; Druze men were included in military conscription in 1956, and separate Druze religious courts were established in 1961.
After capturing the Golan Heights in 1967, Israel offered citizenship to its Druze inhabitants; most refused.

About 92,000 Bedouin lived in the Negev before 1948; after the war about 11,000 remained inside Israel, from 19 of the original 95 tribes, according to Minority Rights Group and the Israeli-Arab legal centre Adalah.

The remaining Negev Bedouin were concentrated in the siyag ('fence'), an area of about 1.5 million dunams, against some 13 million dunams they had used before; the 1953 Land Acquisition Law and the 1965 Planning and Building Law registered much of their land as state land.
Just over 300,000 Bedouin live in Israel today, about 3% of the population; from the 1960s the state built seven planned townships, beginning with Tel Sheva, Rahat and Kseifa.

Of 46 unrecognized Bedouin villages in the Negev, the state had recognized 11 by about 2011, leaving 35; the Association for Civil Rights in Israel recorded 275 buildings demolished in 2010 and 1,000 in 2011.

In May 2024 Israeli authorities demolished about 47–50 homes in the unrecognized village of Wadi al-Khalil; National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called them illegal constructions and the demolition 'an important step'.
Israel does not recognize the Bedouin as an indigenous people, and official policy treats structures in unrecognized villages as illegal building on state land.

Israel's Circassians, Muslims from the Caucasus, live mainly in two Galilee villages, Kfar Kama (about 2,000, Shapsug) and Rehaniya (about 1,000, Abadzakh), settled at the Ottoman Sultan's request in the late nineteenth century; Circassian men serve in the army and police.

The Samaritans claim descent from Israelites who escaped the Assyrian deportation after 722/721 BCE, keep their own version of the Pentateuch, and hold Mount Gerizim sacred; their temple there was destroyed by John Hyrcanus in 128 BCE.

The Samaritans fell to a low of 146 people in 1917 and numbered 654 in January 2003, 349 in Holon and 305 at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus; the Oslo arrangements placed the Nablus community under Palestinian administration.

disputes.question: How many Bedouin live in unrecognized villages?

positions.view: About 100,000 people in roughly 35 unrecognized villages (Minority Rights Group).
About half of some 300,000 Negev Bedouin, i.e. about 150,000 (Adalah, as reported by Al-Monitor, May 2024).
About 70,000 in the villages (ACRI fact sheet, c. 2011).

disputes.question: Squatters or a dispossessed indigenous population?

positions.view: The state and its ministers treat construction in unrecognized villages as illegal building on state land.

Bedouin and rights groups say the villages predate the state or were placed there by it, and that 35 villages meet every Central Bureau of Statistics test for a settlement except the minister's declaration.

entries.topic: The Old Yishuv and nineteenth-century Jerusalem: the Jewish community before Zionism, and the numbers

claims.text: 'Old Yishuv' is the name for the long-settled Jewish residents of the Land of Israel, as distinct from the 'New Yishuv' of the First Aliyah from 1881 onward; it grew in the eighteenth century mainly through Orthodox groups, including Hasidim and disciples of the Vilna Gaon.
Its life centred on four holy cities, Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias; in the nineteenth century most of its members lived in Jerusalem.

The Old Yishuv lived largely on halukka ('distribution'): donations from Jews abroad, handed out by kollels organized by country of origin or Hasidic affiliation, on which the community became almost completely dependent.

The Sephardi leadership, under a chief rabbi (Hakham Bashi, later Rishon LeZion), was officially recognized by the Ottoman authorities and represented the Jews before them; the Ashkenazi kollels united at the end of the century under a General Committee of Knesset Israel.

The Jewish population of the land was about 7,000 in 1800 and about 27,000 in 1880 by the National Library of Israel's count; most researchers put it at 23,000–26,000 in 1880, about half of them in Jerusalem.
Roughly 60,000 Jews arrived between 1881 and 1914; by the summer of 1918, after wartime expulsions, hunger and disease, 56,000 Jews remained, little more than half the 1914 number.

Justin McCarthy's reconstruction from Ottoman registers counts Ottoman-citizen Jews in Palestine at about 13,000 of 369,000 (1860), 13,942 of 440,850 (1878), 17,991 of 516,131 (1890) and 38,754 of 722,143 (1914); the registers did not include foreign nationals, among them many Jewish immigrants.

Figures compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library (from Oesterreicher and Sinai, 1974) give Jerusalem 7,120 Jews of 15,510 people in 1844, 12,000 of 25,030 in 1876 and 28,112 of 45,420 in 1896, and 33,971 Jews in the British census of 1922.
First neighbourhoods outside Jerusalem's walls were built in the second half of the nineteenth century, associated with Moses Montefiore, Yoel Moshe Salomon and Yehoshua Yellin.
The decline of the Ottoman Empire and the Zionist immigration waves cost the Old Yishuv its leading place among the land's Jews.

In a letter to the UN Secretary-General of 1 March 1971 (S/10138), Israel's ambassador Yosef Tekoah cited 28,000 Jews of 43,000 people in the city of Jerusalem in 1887 (Baedeker, 1894), 40,000 of 60,000 in 1905 (Encyclopaedia Britannica, 13th ed.), 33,971 of 62,578 at the 1922 census, 51,222 of 90,503 in 1931 and 97,000 of 157,080 in 1944 (Survey of Palestine).

The Israeli letter answered a letter of 22 February 1971 from Jordan and the United Arab Republic (S/10130), arguing that the Arab figures described the whole Jerusalem sub-district rather than the city.

The same Israeli letter states that Jordan destroyed the Jewish Quarter of the Old City in 1948, including 39 synagogues and places of learning, expelled its Jews, and barred Jewish access to the holy places between 1948 and 1967.

disputes.question: Was Jerusalem a Jewish-majority city before Zionism, and what follows from it?

positions.view: Pro-Israel writers (Stephen Flatow, Jerusalem Post, 2023) cite visitors' calculations showing a Jewish plurality from the mid-1800s and the 1922 census showing Jews as the majority of the city, as evidence of a long Jewish claim to Jerusalem.

Israel's official position (UN letter S/10138, 1971): Jews were the majority of the city itself in 1922, 1931 and 1944 and for decades before the Mandate; Jordan and the United Arab Republic, in S/10130, used figures for the wider Jerusalem sub-district, in which Arabs were the majority.

The nineteenth-century figures come from visitors' estimates and secondary compilations, not a systematic census, and many Jewish residents were foreign subjects outside the Ottoman registers; the analyst Seth Frantzman (2016) stresses that the Jews of nineteenth-century Jerusalem were largely Sephardi and religious, and that the city was a Middle Eastern one.

entries.topic: Who may become a citizen: the Law of Return (1950), the Nationality Law (1952) and the family-unification ban (2003–2022)

claims.text: The Knesset passed the Law of Return on 5 July 1950; Section 1 reads 'Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh', and Section 2 requires the visa to be granted unless the minister finds the applicant is acting against the Jewish people or likely to endanger public health or state security.

An amendment of 23 August 1954 added an exception for a person with a criminal past likely to endanger public welfare, and moved the power from the Minister of Immigration to the Minister of the Interior.

Amendment No. 2 of 10 March 1970 extended the law's rights to the child and grandchild of a Jew and to their spouses and the spouse of a Jew, except a person who had been a Jew and voluntarily changed religion (Section 4A), and defined a Jew as a person born of a Jewish mother or converted to Judaism and not a member of another religion (Section 4B).

The Nationality Law came into force on 14 July 1952. It grants citizenship by return to every oleh under the Law of Return, and by residence to a former Palestinian citizen only if he was registered as an inhabitant on 1 March 1952, was an inhabitant on the day the law took effect, and had been in Israel continuously from the state's establishment or entered legally.

Naturalization under the 1952 law requires, among other things, three years' residence out of the previous five, a right to permanent residence, some knowledge of Hebrew and renunciation of prior nationality.

The Citizenship and Entry into Israel Law, passed in 2003 during the Second Intifada as a one-year temporary measure, generally barred residence permits for Palestinians from the territories married to Israelis, and later for citizens of Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq; it was extended at least 17 times.

Israel's Supreme Court upheld the law 6–5 in 2006 (HCJ 7052/03), although a majority found it disproportionately harmed family life and equality, and rejected a second challenge by one vote in 2012 (HCJ 466/07).

Interior Ministry data for 2020 showed about 800–1,000 family-unification applications a year and about 13,000 Palestinians in Israel on permits or temporary status; 45 Palestinians who received status through family unification were linked to terror offences between 2001 and 2020, none in 2018–2020.

The law lapsed in July 2021 when the Knesset failed to extend it, and was re-enacted on 10 March 2022 by 45 votes to 15, with right-wing opposition votes; the new version states that its aim includes protecting Israel's Jewish majority.
After the 2022 vote Interior Minister Ayelet Shaked called the law a victory for a 'Jewish and democratic state' over 'a state of all its citizens'; Meretz and Ra'am voted against.

Christian Joppke and Zeev Rosenhek (2001) compare Israel's Jewish-priority immigration with West Germany's admission of ethnic-German 'resettlers': about 1.4 million resettlers arrived in 1950–87 and 2.2 million in 1988–97, until a 1993 German law ended the status for those born after 1 January 1993 and capped arrivals.

In the same study, 65% of Israel's Jewish population was foreign-born at the 1948 census, net migration supplied nearly half of Jewish population growth from 1948 to 1995, and about 170,000 of 700,000–900,000 Palestinians remained after 1948–49.

Joppke and Rosenhek report that non-Jews under the halakhic definition made up nearly 20% of immigrants in 1990–94, rising to 45% in 1997 and 53% in 1998, as the 1970 grandchild clause took effect, and that 64% of Jewish Israelis in a survey of the time supported the Law of Return.

disputes.question: Is the Law of Return a legitimate refuge law or a discriminatory one?

positions.view: Defenders (e.g. Alex Stein, 2013) argue it restores Jewish access to the homeland lost since 70 CE and provides a refuge, because states with non-Jewish majorities did not reliably protect their Jews.

Critics, including Palestinian advocates, point out that Palestinian refugees and their descendants cannot return while any Jew may immigrate; the Arab-Israeli legal centre Adalah lists the law in its database of discriminatory laws.

Comparative scholarship (Joppke and Rosenhek, 2001) treats it as one case of 'ethnic-priority immigration' alongside Germany's, explaining its survival by the demographic rivalry with Palestinians and the memory of the Holocaust rather than by ethnic nationhood alone.

disputes.question: Was the 2003 family-unification ban a security measure or a demographic one?

positions.view: Security: the government's explanatory notes and the State Attorney argued that status through marriage could be exploited for terror; Shin Bet testimony cited about 48 such cases in 2001–2021.

Demographic: some supporters said in Knesset debate that the aim was to prevent large-scale Palestinian settlement, the 2022 text names the Jewish majority, and critics say it discriminates against Arab citizens, who are more likely to marry Palestinians; some justices doubted the security case given the small numbers.

entries.topic: The numbers today: Israel's and Jerusalem's populations by group, with 1967 for comparison

claims.text: At the end of 2023 Israel's population was 9,699,200, of whom 7,631,800 (78.7%) were Jews and others and 2,067,300 (21.3%) Arabs, according to Table III/1 of the Statistical Yearbook of Jerusalem.
In 1967 Israel's population was 2,776,300, of whom 392,700 (14.1%) were Arabs.
Jerusalem had 980,700 residents at the end of 2023: 589,300 (60.1%) Jews and others and 391,400 (39.9%) Arabs.
At the end of 1967 Jerusalem had 266,300 residents: 197,700 (74.2%) Jews and others and 68,600 (25.8%) Arabs; at the end of 2022 the figures were 968,700, with 585,700 (60.5%) and 383,000 (39.5%).

entries.topic: How the Holocaust is taught in American schools, 2020–2026

claims.text: The Never Again Education Act (H.R. 943) was signed on Friday, May 29, 2020. It requires the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum to develop and disseminate resources to improve awareness and understanding of the Holocaust, and authorizes Holocaust education programs for prospective and current teachers and educational leaders.

The Government Accountability Office reported to the House and Senate appropriations subcommittees for Labor, Health and Human Services and Education on July 7, 2026 (GAO-26-108023, 'K–12 Education: How States and the U.S. Holocaust Museum Support Holocaust Education'), under a provision in Senate Report 118-84.

GAO found that 43 of 51 states (counting the District of Columbia) have academic standards that explicitly mention the Holocaust or laws requiring it to be taught: 35 include it in standards and 25 require it by law. Eight states have neither: Kansas, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Washington and Wyoming.

Requirements vary widely. Arizona's law requires at least three class periods, or the equivalent, on at least two occasions between seventh and twelfth grade; Florida's standards run from fifth through twelfth grade; New Hampshire's standards mention the Holocaust in a single world-history standard; Michigan's law covers grades 8–12 and names both the Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide. GAO gives no typical number of hours: state officials said teachers 'had to choose which parts of the Holocaust to cover.'

The earliest state requirements listed by Echoes & Reflections are California (1985, grades 7–12), Illinois (1990, expanded 2005), New Jersey (March 1994) and New York (1996, amended 2022); most of the others date from 2016 onward.

Who supplies the classroom material, per GAO: 35 states use materials from local or state Holocaust museums and centers, 34 use materials from the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and 20 use materials from state Holocaust commissions; 10 of 48 responding states write their own and none require schools to use them. 56 of 70 teachers who acquired materials found them on their own. GAO names Echoes & Reflections as a partnership of the Anti-Defamation League, USC Shoah Foundation and Yad Vashem.

Teacher preparation is the main gap GAO found: only 3 of 48 states require Holocaust-specific teacher training; 41 of 48 called teacher preparedness very or somewhat challenging, 39 insufficient time, 37 funding and 34 misinformation. The museum received $2 million under the Never Again Education Act in fiscal year 2025. GAO's report does not mention Israel.

Echoes & Reflections was announced in 2005 by the Anti-Defamation League, the Shoah Visual History Foundation and Yad Vashem, which J. Weekly described as 'Israel's Holocaust Remembrance Authority': ten lessons with maps, photographs, timelines and primary sources, and 51 video testimonies from the Shoah Foundation's 52,000 interviews, with Yad Vashem supplying historical expertise and the ADL handling outreach to schools and state officials.

Its lesson 'Antisemitism after the Holocaust', for middle and high school, lists as a learning objective: 'Identify current features of antisemitism including Holocaust denial and distortion, and demonization of Israel.'

Yad Vashem became a body of the State of Israel by the Yad Vashem Law, brought to the Knesset on 18 May 1953 and passed on 19 August 1953; it had operated privately since 1946. Its mandate includes representing the State of Israel at national and international commemorations; the Knesset limited it to the Holocaust and the destroyed communities, not the rebuilding of the homeland.

In a survey of 1,350 Americans aged 18 to 39 commissioned by the Claims Conference and compiled by Schoen Cooperman Research in early 2020, 63% did not know that six million Jews were murdered (37% chose six million; 15% chose two million), 36% could not name a camp, 12% said the number who died had been 'greatly exaggerated', 90% said the Holocaust happened and 49% had seen Holocaust denial online. The Berkeley sociologist Samuel Lucas cautioned that 'not sure' answers and question wording are hard to interpret, and that social-desirability bias could make denial look smaller than it is.

On 5 July 2025 delegates at the National Education Association's Representative Assembly narrowly adopted a new business item (NBI 39) saying the union would not use, endorse or publicize Anti-Defamation League materials or programs; because it called for a boycott it went to the union's executive committee, which rejected it on 18 July 2025. NEA president Becky Pringle said the boycott 'would not further NEA's commitment to academic freedom, our membership, or our goals.' The item's sponsor, Judy Greenspan, argued that the ADL's definition of antisemitism had made real antisemitism harder to track and fight.

disputes.question: Should Holocaust education include lessons on present-day hostility to Israel as a form of antisemitism?

positions.view: Yes: the ADL's Echoes & Reflections lesson teaches students to identify 'demonization of Israel' among current features of antisemitism, and the NEA's leadership kept the ADL as a partner, saying a boycott would not serve academic freedom.

No, or not on the ADL's terms: the teachers who sponsored the 2025 NEA boycott item argued that the ADL's definition folds criticism of Israel into antisemitism and makes real antisemitism harder to fight.

entries.topic: Where 'Never Again' comes from, and its two meanings

claims.text: The first use of 'Never Again' is murky. JTA traced it most likely to postwar Israel: the phrase appeared in secular kibbutzim in the late 1940s and in a Swedish Holocaust documentary in 1961, and some trace it to Isaac Lamdan's 1926 Hebrew poem 'Masada', with its line 'Never shall Masada fall again!'

Meir Kahane gave the phrase its English currency: he founded the Jewish Defense League in 1968 and titled his 1972 manifesto 'Never Again'. For Kahane it meant 'that if it happens again, it won't happen in the same way'; he used it to justify acts of terror against antisemitism. After his assassination in November 1990, Sholom Comay, president of the American Jewish Committee, said Kahane 'must always be remembered for the slogan Never Again.'

The phrase later took a universal meaning: Barack Obama said in 2011 that it should be 'not just a phrase but a principled cause'; the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum made it the theme of its 2013 Days of Remembrance; Elie Wiesel wrote in 2012 that it 'becomes more than a slogan: It's a prayer, a promise, a vow.' In 2010 Benjamin Netanyahu used both senses: at Auschwitz, 'never again will we allow the hand of evil to sever the life of our people'; in the Rwanda genocide memorial's guestbook, simply 'Never again.'

disputes.question: Does 'Never Again' mean never again for Jews, or never again for anyone?

positions.view: Particular: in Kahane's use it was a call to militancy as the only act of prevention (Shaul Magid's reading), and leaders have used it to mean the protection of the Jewish people specifically.

Universal: Holocaust museums, Wiesel and others use it as a vow against genocide anywhere, and it has been taken up for refugees, Japanese-American internment and other causes; the historian Hasia Diner argues that objecting to such uses is not by itself reasonable.

entries.topic: After the Holocaust: the survivors and Palestine, 1945

claims.text: Earl G. Harrison's team visited 30 displaced-persons camps in Germany and Austria in 1945 and found Jewish survivors held under armed guard behind barbed wire; he wrote that 'we appear to be treating the Jews as the Nazis treated them, except that we do not exterminate them.' He delivered the report to President Truman on 24 August 1945; the White House released it on 29 September.

Harrison reported that most Jewish displaced persons wanted to go to Palestine and cited the Jewish Agency's petition for 100,000 additional immigration certificates. Truman asked Prime Minister Clement Attlee to admit 100,000; Attlee refused. Truman's directive of 22 December 1945 gave displaced persons preference within existing US quotas, and about 22,950 entered the United States over two years, roughly two-thirds of them Jewish.

entries.topic: How the Holocaust is taught outside the United States, country by country, and what people around the world know about it

claims.text: The 2015 UNESCO / Georg Eckert Institute global mapping analysed 272 curricula valid in 2013-2014 from 135 of a possible 195 countries, plus 89 textbooks from 26 countries published since 2000.

The UNESCO study's summary reports that the Holocaust appears in the history curricula of approximately half of the countries investigated, and that about a quarter of all curricula do not name the Holocaust but refer to its context, such as the Second World War or National Socialism.

According to a report on the study in The Conversation, 57 curricula directly stipulate the Holocaust using words such as 'Holocaust' or 'Shoah', eight countries address it only partially, and 46 provide only the context of World War II or National Socialism.
The UNESCO summary found that most curricula do not specify which victim groups to cover, and where groups are named, Jews are usually the only ones explicitly listed.

The UNESCO summary gives Brunei Darussalam, Iceland and Thailand as examples of curricula with no reference to the Holocaust, while the Conversation report on the same study names Egypt, Palestine, Iraq, New Zealand and Thailand as making no reference.

The UNESCO summary lists Argentina, Belize, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico and Slovenia as countries whose curricula refer to the Holocaust only partially, framing it as a human-rights violation; in Mexico it is mentioned as one aspect among others of human-rights education.

The UNESCO textbook analysis found the Holocaust generally located spatially in 'Europe' and 'Germany', while Russian and Indian textbooks cast it in transcontinental terms, setting Europe against Asia.

The UNESCO study reports that Rwandan textbooks apply Holocaust vocabulary to the 1994 genocide, and that Chinese textbooks use the terms 'genocide' (datusha) and 'kinds of crimes' (zhongzhong zuixing) rather than 'Holocaust' or 'Shoah', applying such language to the 1937 Nanjing massacres.
The UNESCO study's authors concluded that "educational media provide a foundation not for education about the Holocaust, but for education about the Holocausts."

Germany's Conference of Education Ministers (KMK) states that the Holocaust and National Socialism are firmly anchored in the History (or history-heavy social-science) curricula of all 16 Länder, as a mandatory topic in grades 9 or 10 of lower secondary school (occasionally grade 8) and a mandatory, more in-depth topic in upper secondary.

KMK recommendations on the subject date back to 20 April 1978 ('Behandlung des Nationalsozialismus im Unterricht'); its 'Erinnern für die Zukunft' recommendations on memory culture were issued on 11 December 2014, and in October 2013 the KMK signed a declaration of intent with Yad Vashem and Israel's education ministry.

Bavaria announced in May 2025 that from the 2025/26 school year students at all secondary schools must visit a concentration-camp memorial at least once during their schooling; previously the requirement applied only to Gymnasium and Realschule students.

Directors of the Buchenwald, Sachsenhausen, Dachau, Bergen-Belsen and Neuengamme memorials were reported in April 2024 as opposing or doubting compulsory school visits, while the Flossenbürg memorial's director reported very good experience with obligatory visits.

Federal Education Minister Karin Prien called in May 2025 for compulsory memorial visits for school students; the International Auschwitz Committee responded that funding for school trips and teacher training mattered more than compulsion.

Israel's Knesset passed a law on 4 March 1959 requiring public observances in tribute to Holocaust victims on Holocaust Remembrance Day, and a 1961 amendment required places of entertainment to close on the eve of the day.

In October 2013 Israeli Education Minister Shai Piron announced a Yad Vashem-designed programme of Holocaust lessons in each of the 12 years of compulsory schooling, starting in first grade; at the time students began in-depth Holocaust study only in 11th grade.

Israel suspended its school trips to Poland in June 2022 amid a dispute in which, per Notes from Poland, the Polish government was reportedly trying to dictate what could be taught; before the pandemic tens of thousands of Israeli youths visited Poland each year.

Polish officials argued the trips strengthened false stereotypes and objected to armed Israeli security guards; the 22 March 2023 agreement to resume them added Polish history and Jewish heritage, meetings with Polish youth, and host-country responsibility for security.

Yad Vashem criticised the 2023 Israel-Poland agreement in April 2023, saying its recommended site list included sites that should not be visited in an educational context and that it had no input into the list.
UCL describes the genocide of European Jews as having been a mandatory subject in the Key Stage 3 National Curriculum for History in England since 1991.

England's current statutory History programme of study (published 11 September 2013) lists, under Key Stage 3, 'In addition to studying the Holocaust' as part of the 'challenges for Britain' content; the Holocaust Educational Trust notes academies need not follow the National Curriculum and that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have no formal requirement.

The UCL Centre for Holocaust Education's October 2016 study of more than 8,000 11-18-year-olds in England found only 37% knew what 'antisemitism' means, 8.8% correctly identified the pre-war German Jewish population as under 1%, and only 7% understood that the June 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union triggered organised mass killing.

The same UCL study found 55% thought the mass murder took place in Germany, 71% associated Auschwitz with the Holocaust (15% each for Treblinka and Bergen-Belsen), and fewer than 10% suggested the German people bore any responsibility.

France's education ministry stated in an answer published 16 April 2019 that the genocides of Jews and Roma are taught for the first time in CM2 (final primary year), that two parts of the troisième (age 14-15) programme address antisemitism and the genocide of the Jews, and that the genocide is studied in the vocational-track première programme.

Poland's February 2018 amendment to its Institute of National Remembrance law, signed by President Andrzej Duda, provided prison sentences of up to three years for accusing Poland of complicity in the Holocaust; on 27 June 2018 both houses of parliament voted to remove the prison penalty, leaving such cases as civil offences subject to fines.

A joint statement by the Polish and Israeli prime ministers accompanying the June 2018 change said they "acknowledge and condemn every single case of cruelty against Jews perpetrated by Poles during the World War II."
A 2008 joint study by the Russian Academy of Sciences and the Russian Jewish Congress found that many Russian school history textbooks completely avoid the subject of the Holocaust.

Historian Ilya Altman of Russia's Holocaust Center told a 1999 Yad Vashem conference that the Holocaust was omitted from Soviet school and university textbooks from the mid-1940s to the late 1980s, that wartime reports replaced 'Jews' with 'peaceful Soviet citizens', and that post-Soviet textbooks mentioned the six million only in passing.

A 2024 study of the 2023 Medinsky-Torkunov grade 10-11 Russian history textbooks, which frame the war as the Great Patriotic War, found no discussion of the Holocaust; the only Jewish reference noted was Tsezar Kunikov listed among Soviet heroes.

In April 2025 Russia promulgated a law defining 'genocide against the Soviet people' during World War II, to enter into force on 1 January 2026; the report on it does not mention Jews or the Holocaust.

Iran's government-sponsored conference questioning the Holocaust opened on 11 December 2006 at the Foreign Ministry's Institute for Political and International Studies in Tehran; Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki said its aim was "not to deny or confirm the Holocaust," and participants included David Duke.
Samira Alayan's 2016 peer-reviewed study in Comparative Education Review found no mention of the Holocaust in Palestinian Authority history textbooks and compared them with Arab-Israeli curricula.

The EU-commissioned Georg Eckert Institute study of Palestinian textbooks (156 of 309 volumes, published June 2021) found UNESCO-style human-rights content alongside 'anti-Semitic narratives and glorifications of violence'; its published FAQ does not address the Holocaust.
The advocacy group IMPACT-se reported on 1 May 2024 that in Saudi textbooks 'The Holocaust is absent from the curriculum.'

The UAE's Washington embassy said in January 2023 that the UAE would include the Holocaust in the curriculum for primary and secondary schools, with the education ministry consulting Yad Vashem and IMPACT-se; Yad Vashem said the initiative was still being developed.

Morocco's Education Minister Said Amzazi announced at a UN General Assembly round table in September 2018 that King Mohammed VI had decided to integrate the study of the Holocaust into the national curriculum.

Argentina's Priority Learning Cores (NAP), approved by the Federal Council of Education Ministers in 2004, list the Holocaust as a topic; Argentina has been a full IHRA member since 2002 and is described by its foreign ministry as the only Latin American full member.

Argentina's Córdoba province has had a provincial Shoah-teaching law since about 2008, under which more than 2,000 teachers have been trained, and in 2026 it added mandatory analysis of hate speech and terrorism.

South Africa's national History curricula for Grades 9 and 11 have included the study of Nazi Germany and the Holocaust since 2007, according to the South African Jewish Board of Deputies' report on the SA Holocaust & Genocide Foundation.
The ADL Global 100 survey (53,100 adults in 102 countries and territories, July 2013-February 2014) found only 54% globally had ever heard of the Holocaust, compared with 94% in Western Europe.

According to NBC News' report on the 2014 ADL survey, 32% of respondents believed the Holocaust was a myth or greatly exaggerated, and only 38% in the Middle East/North Africa region had heard of it, of whom 63% doubted it or considered it exaggerated.

ADL's 2025 Global 100 (over 58,000 adults in 103 countries and territories, fieldwork 23 July-13 November 2024) found 20% worldwide had not heard of the Holocaust and 48% recognised its historical accuracy, falling to 39% among ages 18-34, 16% in the Middle East and North Africa and 23% in Sub-Saharan Africa.

The Claims Conference's eight-country survey (1,000 adults each in the US, UK, France, Austria, Germany, Poland, Hungary and Romania; fieldwork 15-28 November 2023; released January 2025) found that across the European countries 93.5% had heard the word 'Holocaust', 44% knew about 6 million Jews killed, and 81% could name a camp or ghetto.

In that Claims Conference survey, 46% of 18-29-year-olds in France had not heard of the Holocaust (or were unsure), versus 15% in Romania, 14% in Austria and 12% in Germany; and 53% of young Romanians said the number killed had been greatly exaggerated.
A January 2023 Claims Conference survey of 2,000 Dutch adults found 23% of those born after 1980 believed the Holocaust was a myth or that the number of victims was greatly exaggerated.

UN General Assembly resolution 60/7, adopted 1 November 2005, designated 27 January as an annual International Day of Commemoration, urged Member States to develop educational programmes on the Holocaust's lessons, and "Rejects any denial of the Holocaust as an historical event, either in full or part."

UN General Assembly resolution 76/250 on Holocaust denial, sponsored by Israel and co-sponsored by 114 nations, was adopted by consensus without a vote on 20 January 2022; Iran disassociated itself from it.

The IHRA, founded in 1998 on the Stockholm Declaration (which pledges to promote Holocaust education in schools and universities), states it has 35 Member Countries and 8 Observer Countries, and in 2019 published Recommendations for Teaching and Learning about the Holocaust organised around why, what and how to teach.

disputes.question: Should visits to concentration-camp memorials be compulsory for German students?

positions.view: Yes: Bavaria made them compulsory for all secondary schools from 2025/26 and Federal Minister Karin Prien called for compulsory visits; the Flossenbürg memorial reports good experience with obligatory visits.

No: directors of Buchenwald, Sachsenhausen, Dachau, Bergen-Belsen and Neuengamme argued voluntariness is essential and coercion can reinforce rejection; the International Auschwitz Committee stressed funding and teacher training over compulsion.

disputes.question: How should Israeli school trips to Poland be structured?

positions.view: Polish government: the trips focused narrowly on the war, strengthened negative stereotypes of Poles and used armed guards; they should include Polish history and Jewish heritage.
Yad Vashem: the 2023 agreement's site list included educationally inappropriate sites; trips must keep complete historical accuracy, including Poles' roles in both persecuting and rescuing Jews.

disputes.question: Poland's 2018 law on attributing Nazi crimes to the Polish nation

positions.view: Polish government: those who say Poland may be responsible for WWII crimes deserve penalties (PM Morawiecki); the law defended Poland's reputation.
Critics in Israel, the US and Europe, including the World Jewish Congress: the law whitewashed history and stifled discussion of local complicity; the prison penalty was removed in June 2018.
